2 
 
 
 
Summary: Competition law – appeal – interim relief in terms of  s 49C of the 
Competition Act 89 of 1998 (the Act) – whether t he Competition Tribunal correctly 
dismissed the application on the basis that the appellant failed to establish its market 
definition and failed to make out a prima facie case of abuse of dominance under s 8 
of the Act – whether the requirements of s 49C(2)(b) of the Act were established.  
3 
 
 
 
ORDER 
 
 
An appeal from: The decision of the Competition Tribunal: 
1. The appeal is upheld with costs, including the costs of two counsel; 
2. The decision of the Tribunal dismissing the application is set aside and replaced 
with the following order with effect from date of this order: 
‘1 For a period of six months from the date of this order, or the conclusion of a 
hearing in respect of the prohibited practices alleged by the applicants in the 
complaint filed with the Competition Commission under case number 
2025FEB0007, whichever is the earlier: 
1.1 The first respondent is directed to reinstate the second applicant’s access 
permissions and on-site storage at Mediclinic Vergelegen, Mediclinic Morningside, 
Mediclinic Panorama, Mediclinic Potchefstroom and Mediclinic Newcastle (the 
hospitals) on the same bases that applied at the time when the second applicant 
operated at the hospitals, and to ensure that the second applicant is permitted to 
administer renal dialysis treatment and/or extracorporeal blood -related treatment 
to patients at the hospitals,  where the second applicant has been requested to 
administer such treatment by a referring clinician, subject to the second applicant’s 
substantial adherence to the first respondent’s reasonable infection control, 
security and other protocols;  
1.2 The first respondent is directed to permit the second applicant to continue to 
administer any form of inpatient renal dialysis treatment and/or extracorporeal 
blood-related treatment to patients at all Mediclinic hospitals in South Africa at 
which the second applicant is currently providing services, on the same bases as 
the second applicant currently provides those services, and to refrain from in any 
way preventing or impeding the second applicant from doing so, where the second 
applicant has been requested to administer such treatment by a referring clinician, 
subject to the second applicant’s continued substantial adherence to the first 
respondent’s reasonable infection control, security and other protocols;  
1.3 The first respondent is directed to circulate a communication to all clinicians, 
including but not limited to nephrologists, physicians, nurses and renal 
4 
 
technologists, and to hospital executive and clinical management, at all the 
Mediclinic hospitals at which the second applicant is currently providing services, 
or has been excluded from providing services by the first respondent, explaining 
the nature and meaning of the obligations set out in paragraphs 1.1 and 1.2 above, 
and expressly indicating that all clinicians are free to call for the services of the 
second applicant to treat patients at Mediclinic hospitals, and that they will not 
suffer any repercu ssions as a result of exercising their clinical discretion in this 
regard; and  
1.4 The first respondent is directed to circulate a communication to all employees 
of the second respondent explaining the obligations set out in paragraphs 1.1 and 
1.2 above, and indicating that the second applicant is permitted to treat patients at 
all the Mediclinic hospitals at which it is currently providing services, or has been 
excluded from providing services by the first respondent, and should not be 
prevented or impeded from carrying out services in these hospitals, in any way 
whatsoever.  
1.5 The costs of the application, including the costs of two counsel, shall be paid 
by the respondents, jointly and severally, the one paying, the other to be absolved.’  
  
5 
 
 
 
JUDGMENT 
 
 
Dippenaar AJA (Davis and Phatshoane AJJA concurring) 
 
[1] This is an appeal in terms of s 49C(7) of the Competition Act 89 of 1998 (the 
Act) concerning the dismissal of the  appellants’ application for interim relief under          
s 49C of the Act.  The first appellant is Life Healthcare Group (Pty) Ltd  (Life 
Healthcare). The second appellant is its wholly owned subsidiary, Life Renal Care (Pty) 
Ltd (Life Renal). The first respondent is Mediclinic Southern Africa (Pty) Ltd (Mediclinic 
SA). The second respondent is its wholly owned subsidiary, Mediclinic Renal Services 
South Africa (Pty) Ltd  (Mediclinic Renal) . Where convenient the appellants and 
respondents will collectively be referred to as ‘Life’ and 7Mediclinic’ respectively.  
 
[2] Life Healthcare and Mediclinic SA both operate a number of multidisciplinary 
private hospitals providing acute hospital care. Both Life Renal and Mediclinic Renal 
provide renal dialysis services  in hospitals and standalone clinics. There are three 
large corporate hospital operators in South Africa, Netcare Group Ltd, Life and 
Mediclinic. Netcare is the largest. All three offer dialysis services at their hospitals. 
Historically all three have permitted third party dialysis service providers to operate at 
their hospitals. The extent to which third party providers operated at the various 
hospital groups is in dispute. At these hospitals other services are provided by 
independent third parties, such as doctors, pathologists and the like. These providers 
can compete on both price and quality of service. Mediclinic confirmed that it ‘controls 
access to its own hospitals and can therefore prevent a downstream competitor from 
providing services at its own hospitals’. 
6 
 
[3] It was common cause that there is a category of in -hospital patients who are 
acute patients, such as emergency patients 1 and crash landers. 2 Both acute and 
chronic inpatients receive treatment whilst confined to a hospital. The decision as to 
which service provider a patient is referred to typically rests with the patient’s 
nephrologist or specialist physician. That referral decision is exerci sed with clinical 
independence and is primarily informed by the perceived quality of care provided by a 
particular dialysis services provider. The administration of dialysis services requires a 
renal technologist or a renal nurse. There is no material differences in equipment used 
to administer treatment to chronically ill and acutely ill patients. Both acute and chronic 
patients receive treatment whilst confined to a hospital, often in its intensive care unit, 
and so are limited to receiving dialysis services from in-hospital units and mobile units. 
 
[4] At the beginning of 2024, Life Healthcare expanded Life Renal’s business by 
acquiring the dialysis business of a third party, Fresenius (Pty) Ltd  (Fresenius). 
Fresenius had entered the market during 2001 as an independent.  The Competition 
Commission approved the Life/Fresenius merger with effect from 1 April 2024. One of 
the agreed conditions of the Life Fresenius merger was that Life would continue to 
permit third party dialysis service providers access to its hospitals.  
 
[5] Mediclinic in turn, acquired a 79% interest in another dialysis service provider , 
BGM Renal Care (Pty) Ltd  (BGM), and established the Mediclinic Renal. BGM was 
created in 2020 by Mr Prinsloo, the previous CEO of Fresenius. For a period after the 
Life/Fresenius acquisition both Life Renal and Mediclinic Renal provided in-hospital 
dialysis services at certain of Mediclinic’s hospitals and competed on this level. From 
about January 2024  and shortly prior to Life’s acquisition  of Fresenius , Mediclinic 
began rolling out its strategy to insource the provision of dialysis services in its 
hospitals, targeting Life Rena l’s operations at its hospitals. The affected Mediclinic 
hospitals are Vergelegen  (Somerset West) , Pan orama (Panorama in Cape Town) , 
Morningside (Sandton), Potchefstroom and Newcastle.  Mediclinic Renal established 
 
1 Being patients who were not previously treated with dialysis but who are admitted to hospital on an 
inpatient basis as a result of an acute episode and who require dialysis during their hospitalisation. They 
may require dialysis owing to a catastrophic ev ent which causes his or her kidneys to shut down, but 
he or she is anticipated to regain normal kidney function over time such that ongoing dialysis treatment 
on an outpatient basis is not required. 
2 Being patients who are admitted to hospital after a sudden and unexplained deterioration in their health 
and are then for the first time diagnosed with kidney disease.  
7 
 
its own operations alongside those of Life Renal and then gave Life Renal notice that 
it was terminating Life Renal’s access to the hospital, effectively ending its ability to 
provide services in the hospital. Mediclinic Renal then stepped in and took over all the 
services Life Renal had been providing at the hospital.  
 
[6] This conduct led Life lodging a complaint of abuse of dominance  with the 
Competition Commission on 6 February 2025. Its case is that Mediclinic  is engaging 
in various exclusionary acts  in terms of s 8 of the Act ; in particular i n terms of s 
8(1)(d)(i), in preventing dialysis patients and their referring  doctors from dealing with 
a competitor of Mediclinic Renal ; requiring that patients  admitted to a Mediclinic 
hospital must obtain dialysis services from Mediclinic Renal in contravention of 
s  8(1)(d)(iii); and /or that Mediclinic  is otherwise engaging in exclusionary conduct  
where the anti -competitive conduct is not outweighed by any alleged efficiency 
benefits in contravention of s 8(i)(c). Life alleges that Mediclinic is seeking to foreclose 
the market and prevent the provision of in -house dialysis services by third party 
dialysis service providers at Mediclinic’s multidisciplinary hospitals. The complaint is 
presently still being investigated by the Commission. 
 
[7] Life sought interim interdictory relief in terms of s 49C from the Competition 
Tribunal (Tribunal) by way of an application launched on 17 April 2025 .3 That 
application forms the subject matter of this appeal. Some six months after the hearing, 
on 23 February 2026, the majority of the Tribunal members dismissed the application. 
The majority (Prof Valodia and Ms Ndoni) held that Life had failed to make out a prima 
facie case that: (a) there was a distinct market for the provision of dialysis services to 
patients in hospitals; and (b) Mediclinic’s dominance in the market. According to the 
majority, the market definition advanced by Mediclinic, being the provision of services 
in multidisciplinary hospitals, was more plausible than that of Life as dialysis services 
simply formed one aspect of the broad market for the provision of acute 
multidisciplinary private hospital services. The majority did not regard it necessary to 
consider the other factors in s 49C(2) (b) and dismissed the application on the basis 
that no prima facie case of abuse of dominance had been made out by Life.  
 
3The application was argued on 25 August 2025. Further submissions were made on 9 September 
2025. 
8 
 
[8] The minority (Mr Wessels), took issue with those findings, concluding that Life 
had established a prima facie case of abuse of dominance and that the majority had 
failed to consider the matter from the perspective of the constitutional imperatives as 
set out in Competition Commission of South Africa v Mediclinic Southern Africa (Pty) 
Ltd and Another (Mediclinic).4 In the written reasons provided for the order, neither the 
majority nor the minority dealt with all the requirements of s 49C(2)(b) of the Act. 
 
[9] This appeal is based on the following grounds: (a) that the Tribunal failed to 
consider all the factors in s 49C(2)(b) as it only considered the issue in s 49C(2)(b)(i); 
(b) that the Tribunal failed to have regard to the  constitutionally entrenched right of 
access to healthcare; (c) that the Tribunal erred in relation to market definition; (d) 
dominance and market power; (e) exclusionary conduct and anti -competitive effect; 
and (f) its view on the effect of the decision. It was common cause that the Tribunal’s 
order is appealable. 
 
[10] The stance adopted by Life was that it has accepted that any dialysis service 
provider should be allowed to operate at its hospitals if there is a request for them to 
do so, having agreed to such condition when it acquired Fresenius as part of the 
merger conditions  (the open access condition) . Life considers this to be standard 
industry practice. Its view is that each hospital constitutes a separate market and that 
Mediclinic’s conduct is exclusionary and falls within the prohibitions on abusive  
dominance in that market as envisaged by s 8 of the Act, Mediclinic being a dominant 
firm as envisaged by s 7 of the Act.  
 
[11] Mediclinic adopted the opposite stance, namely that ‘for as long as patients are 
admitted to Mediclinic, Life cannot treat them’. It s intention is to insource its renal 
dialysis and related services at its hospitals, a strategy which will be implemented over 
time at all its hospitals. Mediclinic’s case is that Life’s case for dominance is contrived, 
its market definition is flawed and its theory of harm devoid of factual underpinning. 
The parties adopted the same stance in the appeal as before the Tribunal. 
 
 
4Competition Commission of South Africa v Mediclinic Southern Africa (Pty) Ltd and Another  [2021] 
ZACC 35; 2022 (4) SA 323 (CC); 2022 (5) BCLR 532 (CC) (Mediclinic). 
9 
 
[12] Section 49C of the Act regulates interim relief. In relevant part, s 49C provides:  
‘(2) The Competition Tribunal –  
. . .  
(b) may grant an interim order if it is reasonable and just to do so, having regard to the following 
factors:  
(i) The evidence relating to the alleged prohibited practice;  
(ii) the need to prevent serious or irreparable damage to the applicant; and  
(iii) the balance of convenience.  
(3) I n any proceedings in terms of this section, the standard of proof is the same as the 
standard of proof in a High Court on a common law application for an interim interdict.’ 
 
[13] It is well established that all three factors must be considered holistically  and 
must be weighed and balanced through the prism of what is reasonable and just. 5 As 
held in Business Connexion (Pty) Ltd v Vexall (Pty) Ltd and Another (Business 
Connexion):6 
‘The evidence of a prohibited practice is not concerned with the rights of an applicant but the 
competitive position of competitors in the market, judged against the regulatory criteria of the 
prohibited practices defined in chapter 2 of the Act’.  
 
[14] The need to prevent serious or irreparable damage to an applicant posits an 
enquiry into the effects of the alleged  prohibited practice upon the applicant and is a 
party specific enquiry.7 Damage is to the competitive position of an applicant and other 
forms of damage are not relevant.  The balance of convenience requires that ‘the 
currency of prejudice is reckoned by recourse to the consequences of the competitive 
positioning of the parties in the market’.8  
 
[15] The approach to be adopted is to first establish if there is evidence of a 
prohibited practice, the Act’s analogue of a prima facie right. The facts alleged by Life 
must be considered , together with the facts alleged by Mediclinic that Life cannot 
dispute, and then to consider whether having regard to the inherent probabilities, Life 
 
5Business Connexion (Pty) Ltd v Vexall (Pty) Ltd and Another  [2020] 2 CPLR 490 (CAC) (Business 
Connexion) para 19.  
6Ibid para 20. 
7Ibid para 21. 
8Ibid para 22. 
10 
 
should on those facts establish the existence of a prohibited practice at the hearing of 
the complaint referral’.9 
 
[16] As held in GovChat (Pty) Ltd and Another v Facebook Inc, WhatsApp Inc and 
Facebook South Africa (Pty) Ltd (GovChat),10 s 8(1)(c) is a rule of reason prohibition. 
This means that the conduct complained of will be prohibited only if it has an anti -
competitive effect which is not outweighed by pro-competitive justifications. Under s 
8(1)(c) an applicant or complainant must show the elements of the exclusionary 
conduct and that the anti - competitive effects outweigh technological or other 
competitive effects. However, under s 8 (1)(d) once the elements of s 8 (1)(d) are 
satisfied, the onus sh ifts to the respondent to demonstrate that the effects are 
outweighed by pro -competitive gains. Life must show the critical elements, namely 
dominance of Mediclinic and that the conduct complained of has exclusionary effects. 
An assessment of a firm ’s dominance is almost alw ays done with reference to the 
market within which it functions.11  
 
[17] According to  eMedia Investments (Pty) Ltd v Multichoice (Pty) Ltd ,12 s 49C 
envisages that the Tribunal is obliged to make a summary assessment before granting 
the interim relief. The assessment is only at the prima facie level. It must consider the 
evidence as to the alleged practice. There is usually no t ime to delve too deeply into 
theories of irreparable harm but at the very least it must be assessed in the context of 
whether there is a prima facie right at the interim level. As long as there is clear and 
non-speculative evidence about possible anti -competitive effects, then serious 
consideration must be given to gran ting relief. Relief cannot be granted under s  49C 
unless a prima facie case has been established which, in turn implies that an applicant 
has put up an arguable case that the state of competition, that is the competitive 
dynamics in the defined market, can be detrimentally affected by the alleged conduct 
or practice of a respondent.  
 
 
9GovChat (Pty) Ltd and Another v Facebook Inc and Others (case no IR165Nov20) (11 November 2021) 
para 21. 
10Ibid para 27. 
11Ibid par 29 and authorities cited in fn19. 
12eMedia Investments (Pty) Ltd v Multichoice (Pty) Ltd and Other [2023] 3 CPLR 32 (CAC) para 19. 
11 
 
[18] It is thus not contentious that if no prima facie case was made out, the Tribunal 
was entitled to dismiss the application on that basis without considering the other two 
factors.13  
 
[19] The central issue is whether Life established a prima facie case for abuse of 
dominance. The starting point is whether Life established its market definition on a 
prima facie basis. This issue dominated the submissions presented at the hearing. Life 
contended that a separate market exists for the provision of dialysis services to in -
hospital patients in the individual hospitals. Mediclinic on the other hand submitted that 
the well-established market for multi-disciplinary hospital services applied and that the 
provision of dialysis services was simply a component of the provision of 
multidisciplinary private hospital services. The key dispute between the parties is 
whether competition occurs when patients choose a hospital prior to their admission 
or whether a further choice is made once patients are admitted and they require 
dialysis. It was not disputed that if Life’s market definition was accepted on a prima 
facie basis, Mediclinic was a monopolist in each relevant market, given that it owns its 
hospitals and controls access to them. 
 
[20] Mediclinic argued that a patient makes a single purchasing decision prior to 
admission to a multidisciplinary hospital and that the focal product and relevant market 
is that for multidisciplinary hospitals. According to Mediclinic, crash landers and acute 
patients make a single purchasing decision  about which hospital they wish to be 
admitted before they know they need dialysis and that the purchasing decision is 
clearly one between hospitals offering multidisciplinary services made prior to 
admission. It is m ore plausible, so the argument goes , that competitive constraints 
operate at the level of the hospital bundle rather than at the level of distinct  services 
such as dialysis as crash landers or their referring doctors will choose the hospital at 
which they wish to be treated based on the same considerations that any other patient 
(except emergency) will choose a hospital  – convenience and the availability of a 
suitable range of specialist services. For that reason, it is irrelevant whether patients 
 
13Mercantile Bank, A division of Capitec Bank Limited and Others v Surve and Others [2023] ZACAC 2; 
[2023] 3 CPLR 33 (CAC). 
 
12 
 
know in advance if they will require dialysis services as they contract for the provision 
of a holistic service which includes foreseeable and unforeseeable medical services. 
 
[21] According to Mediclinic, even if it is assumed that hospitals provide upstream 
services and that separate services such as dialysis, cardiology and the like are each 
separate non -substitutable downstream services, the relevant question for input 
foreclosure is whether the input provided by Medicli nic is truly an essential facility or 
whether it is substitutable with space at other hospitals or facilities. Patients are not an 
input. The question is whether a renal dialysis provider can use space at other 
hospitals or buildings in the same geographic area to compete effectively with 
Mediclinic Renal. It was submitted that if one is to consider the matter with reference 
to two vertically related market s, the relevant downstream market would be th at for 
renal dialysis services and the upstream market ( the input required to provide such 
services) would be space from which to practice in a given geographic area  and not 
access to ‘captured patients’ . It maintains that it has a constitutional right to control 
access to its own property. Mediclinic further contended that it was not shown to be a 
dominant provider of space within hospitals in a particular geographic area.  
 
[22] According to Mediclinic the market in which private hospitals compete has 
consistently been defined as being that for multidisciplinary services .14 In-hospital 
renal dialysis services is but one aspect of that service offering. In most hospitals the 
hospital group that owns the hospital also provides the dial ysis services inside the 
hospital on an exclusive basis.  It was argued that Life does not explain why dialysis 
services are different or are a specialist discipline. According to Mediclinic, the closest 
the Tribunal has come to departing from that approach is in Mediclinic v Matlosana  
(Matlosana),15 where it acknowledged that hospitals compete on various metrics, 
including quality of care and the provision of a cluster of services and noted that distinct 
inpatient services are not substitutes for each other.16  
 
14Relying on Afrox Healthcare Limited /Amalgamated Hospitals Limited  (53/LM/Sept01) [2001] ZACT 
42; Phodiclinic (Pty) Ltd & Others/Protector Group Medical Services (Pty) Ltd & Others (122/LM/Dec05) 
[2007] ZACT 17 paras 21-24 & 117; Netcare Hospitals (Pty) Ltd v Lakeview Hospitals (IM193Oct17) 
[2018] ZACT 93 paras 10, 12, 17. 
15Mediclinic v Matlosana (LM124Octo16) [2020] JOL 46577 (CT) (Matlosana). 
16In Matlosana, the Tribunal held: 
‘[82] The distinct inpatient hospital services generally are not substitutes for each other. Consequently 
one could delineate each individual inpatient hospital service as a separate relevant product market. 
13 
 
 
[23] Life’s case on the other hand is that there is a distinct class of patients who do 
not make up-front decisions as to which hospital they will attend to obtain dialysis. 
Life’s argument rests on the relevant patient group being primarily the crash landers – 
people who discover they need dialysis only after they are admitted to a hospital. 
Those are the patients who do not make an upfront choice to select their hospital 
based on the price or quality of its dialysis services and cannot, once they have been 
admitted, switch hospitals, even if the dialysis service they are receiving is inferior in 
quality. Life submitted that t hey are an important category of patients for dialysis 
service providers because they will invariably continue to receive dialysis after the ir 
discharge from hospital and whoever initially provided dialysis will have a distinct 
advantage in retaining them as patients once they are discharged. It was not 
contentious that c rash landers are the most important source of referrals of new 
chronic patients.  
 
[24] According to Life, the analysis must start with the service s that are the focal 
point from which to assess the extent to which competitors can and do serve as 
immediate and effective constraints on a firm supplying that service. 17 The existence 
of such a market is supported through application of the well -established tools for 
assessing demand and supply side suitability and the undisputed facts, including the 
actual competition between dialysis service providers for in-house hospital services. It 
was submitted that there is a m arket at each hospital for provision of access to the 
hospital for the provision of these services. Once that is accepted, there can be no 
real dispute that Mediclinic is a dominant firm at each of its hospitals , that it is able to 
exert market power to foreclose rival dialysis service providers from its hospitals and 
that it has in fact done so, with a clear anti-competitive effect in each market. There is 
merit in Life’s approach. 
 
However, doing so would be burdensome and therefore, for analytical convenience, we do not follow 
that approach in this case.  
[83] It was common cause that outpatient services are a separate relevant product market. Outpatient 
services are not substitutable with inpatient hospital services and are offered by a different set of 
competitors under different competitive conditions.  
[84] The economic experts also agreed that specialised hospitals which offer only one discipline, such 
as inpatient psychiatric services, are part of (a) separate relevant product market(s) .’ 
17European Union Commission Notice on the definition of the relevant market for the purposes of Union 
competition law  available at https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-
content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=OJ:C_202401645 accessed on 5 August 2026. 
14 
 
 
[25] The majority of the Tribunal held that it could not apply a small but significant 
non-transitory increase in price ( SSNIP) test and could not determine whether a 
hypothetical monopolist could raise prices or reduce quality to this class of patients  
(crash landers) without them switching hospitals. However, in Matlosana the Tribunal 
held:18 
‘…A medical scheme or uninsured patient cannot substitute an inpatient service for a day care 
service of an acute multi -disciplinary hospital in response to a price increase or quality 
reduction in inpatient services. Put differently, a hypothetical monopolist of inpatient multi -
disciplinary private hospital services could profitably raise prices by a small but significant 
amount or degraded non-price factors without the risk of substitution to the day care services 
of the hospitals.’ 
That lends credence to the Life’s proposed approach. 
 
[26] To determine whether Life has established the market contended for, i t is 
necessary to consider demand -side substitutability and the hypothetical monopolist 
test. The purpose of market definition in complaint proceedings is to identify the 
primary competitive forces relevant to assessing the effects of the conduct by the firm 
that is the subject of the complaint – in particular whether and to what extent there are 
other firms that act as immediate and effective constraints on that firm.19  
 
[27] Applying the hypothetical monopolist test, what must be considered is the 
smallest geographical area over which a hypothetical monopolist could impose and 
sustain a small but significant non -transitory increase in price (SSNIP) or effect a 
deterioration in non-price factors. The ambit of the relevant geographic market thus 
depends on the distance that patients would be willing to travel in the case of a 
hypothetical S SNIP or deterioration in non -price factors at one of the relevant 
hospitals. It is accepted  that there are asymmetrical constraints between inpatients, 
outpatients and day cases. The question is what patients would regard as an 
alternative hospital, if any, in the case of SNIPP or a quality deterioration at a specific 
hospital. 
 
 
18Matlosana fn 17 para 96. 
19eMedia fn 14 para 58. 
15 
 
[28] The smallest possible market is the provision of in-hospital dialysis services at 
Mediclinic’s hospitals. There is no demand -side substitutability for this service for a 
patient in a hospital. Should a patient require dialysis, they must obtain it in a hospital. 
From a patient’s demand-side perspective, there is a specific and identifiable demand 
for dialysis services that can only be provided in -hospital, which is not substitutable 
with services that can be provided outside the hospital. That service is also not 
substitutable either for other specific services provided in the hospital or for the overall 
general suite of services offered by the hospital in which they have been admitted or 
by any other hospital. The lack of demand side substitution is key to delineating the 
relevant market.  
 
[29] Guidance is to be found in the European Union Commission Notice on the 
definition of the relevant market for the purposes of Union Competit ion law (EU 
notice):20  
‘Demand substitution constitutes the most effective and immediate disciplinary force on the 
suppliers of a given product. An undertaking ’s influence over prevailing conditions of sale – 
such as prices, the level of innovation or the quality offered – depends on the extent to which 
its customers can easily  switch to available products that the customers consider as 
substitutes. Demand substitution is therefore the main consideration when defining the 
relevant product market.’  
 
[30] From a supply side perspective, it was undisputed that the only firms that can 
supply dialysis to patients in a hospital are those that have an in -hospital unit within 
that hospital or have a mobile unit that can readily b e moved into that hospital in a 
short period of time. There are no significant technical barriers preventin g a mobile 
unit from providing such services at different hospitals within its operating area as there 
are no material differences in processes, staff and equipment used to administer in- 
hospital dialysis to acute or chronic patients, or to administer in -hospital dialysis 
treatments in different multidisciplinary hospitals. Mobile units are thus capable of 
competing and do compete with in -hospital units operating within a given 
multidisciplinary hospital. In-hospital and mobile units are therefore the only firms that 
 
20According to the EU Notice fn 19 par 23(a); See also para 23(b) of the EU Notice is states that: 
‘Supply substitution can also be relevant for the definition of the relevant market in some cases, namely 
when it is as effective and immediate as demand substitution and when it leads to similar competitive 
conditions across the products concerned.’  
16 
 
can compete in the market. The direct service is access to and storage space in each 
of the various hospitals Mediclinic operates. Once the downstream market for the 
provision of in-hospital dialysis services is correctly identified, then the existence of an 
upstream market for the provision of access to a hospital to provide these services 
appears clear, at least on a prima facie basis.  
 
[31] From a demand side perspective, a firm wishing to provide in-hospital dialysis 
services at a particular hospital must be provided access to and storage facilities in a 
particular hospital. From a supply side perspective, access to and storage facilities at 
a specific hospital can only ever be provided by that particular hospital. Every hospital 
has complete and exclusive control over access to and storage at its premises and 
thus has real monopoly power. Since provision of access permissions and reasonable 
on-site storage facilities to mobile dialysis providers constitutes an essential input into 
the market for in-hospital dialysis services, the two markets are virtually related. This 
gives rise to a classic input foreclosure theory of harm whereby Mediclinic’s 
withholding of access to those essential input s results in the foreclosure of mobile 
dialysis service providers from the market for the provision of those se rvices. The 
markets are at least complementary – sufficient for appellants to establish a leveraging 
theory of harm  – in-house hospital patients are locked in once admitted allowing 
Mediclinic to leverage market power from each market for access to its various  
hospitals to each inpatient dialysis services market. 
 
[32] On the evidence there are several indicators that Mediclinic’s market definition 
is not accurate in the current circumstances.  The respondent’s systems market is 
inconsistent with the EU notice which provides guidance on defining markets involving 
primary and secondary products. There is no demand side substitutability. From a 
patient’s demand side perspective there  is a specific and identifiable demand fro m 
dialysis services that can only be provided in a hospital, which is not substitutable with 
services that can be provided outside the hospital. It is also not substitutable for other 
specific services provided in a hospital or for the overall general suite of services 
offered by the hospital in which they were admitted or by any other hospital. 
 
[33] In considering the anti -competitive effects, it must be consider ed whether the 
exclusionary act is substantial or significant in foreclosing the market to rivals . Those 
17 
 
effects can be actual or potential. Mediclinic’s submissions regarding the replacement 
of one monopoly provider by another and hence that Computicket (Pty) Ltd v 
Competition Commission of South Africa (Computicket)21 is distinguishable (because 
there has been no reduction in the number of service providers ), does not bear 
scrutiny. Factually it was undisputed that both Life Renal and Mediclinic Renal for a 
period of time competed at the respective hospitals. Whether it was a transitiona ry 
period, as Mediclinic contends, does not detract from this fact. 
 
[34] As held in South African Airways (Pty) Ltd v Comair Ltd and Another:22  
‘It was sufficient if there was evidence that the exclusionary practice is substantial or significant 
or it has the potential to foreclose the market to competition. If it is substantial or significant, it 
may be inferred that it creates, enhances or preserves the market power of the dominant firm. 
If it creates, enhances or preserves the market power of the dominant firm it will be assumed 
to have an anti-competitive effect’.  
 
[35] Mediclinic’s contentions of pro-competitive gains, a reduction in revenue to Life 
Renal, safety and clinical considerations, do not bear scrutiny.  In their answering 
papers, Mediclinic raised certain complaints and concerns about the quality of renal 
services provided by Fresenius and gaps in clinical supervision of patients , resulting 
in harm to patients. They placed reliance on affidavits from four former employees of 
Fresenius, who left its employ before the acquisition of Fresenius by Life Renal. It does 
not appear from the papers that any complaints were raised at the time. There is merit 
in Life’s contention that the quality complaints were raised to counter Life’s complaints, 
given that they are historical prior to Life Acquiring Fresenius in 2024 and its own 
inaction in addressing those complaints until Life acquired control before raising such 
complaints, at least on a prima facie basis. Mediclinic’s claim that a reduction in Life’s 
revenue is inherently pro -competitive conflates harm to an incumbent with benefit to 
the competitive proc ess. It is not itself evidence of improved  competitive outcomes. 
The question is not whether Life loses revenue but whether the impugned conduct 
excludes a competitor. Mediclinic’s argument that choice is not reduced because one 
service provider has simply been replaced by another, does not withstand scrutiny. 
 
21Computicket (Pty) Ltd v Competition Commission of South Africa  [2019] 2 CPLR 539 (CAC)  
(Computicket). 
22South African Airways (Pty) Ltd v Comair Ltd and Another  2012 (1) SA 20 (CAC) paras 10 6, quoted 
in Computicket para 19. 
18 
 
Even where Life Renal was the sole provider so that the market was uncontested, it 
was always constrained by the possibility of entry by a new entrant. 
 
[36] The approach adopted by the majority of the Tribunal disregarded two important 
factors. First, in its valuation, the Tribunal was required, as pointed out in the minority 
judgment, to take into account the jurisprudential and transformative principles of the 
Constitution and the Act and to consider the aspir ation to create a social justice - 
sensitive economy,  23 given that the conduct complained of impacts patients ’ 
constitutional right to access to healthcare. 24 Second, the Tribunal was required to 
holistically 25 consider all three factors in s 49C(2)(b), weigh and balance those factors 
through the prism of what is reasonable and just. 26 This was stated by the Tribunal in 
Nedschroef Johannesburg (Pty) Ltd v Teamcor Ltd and Others  (Nedschroef).27 An 
applicant for an interim order need only adduce evidence of a contravention at a prima 
facie level and the Tribunal is required to make a summary assessment of that 
evidence in order to grant interim relief.28 The Tribunal was not required to determine 
whether Life had proved its case, rather whether its case was arguable, and thus 
crossed the prima facie case threshold.29 
 
[37] It is by reference to the impugned conduct and its effects that the relevant 
market ought to be defined. On a prima facie level Life has established the market it 
contends for, even if it is open to some doubt. For present purposes that is sufficient. 
On its face and at least on a prima facie basis, Mediclinic’s conduct is in contravention 
of s 8 of the Act , by using its monopoly power as a provider of access to patients to 
foreclose competitors to its hospitals . Granting interim would preserve competition 
pending the final determination of Life’s complaint.  
 
 
23eMedia Investments (Pty) Ltd South Africa v Multichoice (Pty) Ltd and Another (eMedia  2022) [2022] 
2 CPLR 23 (CAC) para 95. 
24Mediclinic fn 4 para 2. 
25GovChat para 160.  
26Business Connexion (Pty) Ltd v Vexall (Pty) Ltd and Another (Business Connexion)  (2020) 2 CPLR 
490 (CAC) para 19.  
27Nedschroef Johannesburg (Pty) Ltd  and Teamcor Ltd/Waco International Ltd/ CBC Fasteners (Pty) 
Ltd/Avlock International (Pty) Ltd and Others [2006] 1 CPLR 98 (CT) para 24. 
28Mercantile Bank, A Division of Capitec bank Ltd and Others v Surve and Others  [2023] 3 CPLR 33 
(CAC) para 25. 
29eMedia 2022 fn 26 para 19  
19 
 
[38] On a conspectus of the facts, at least on a prima facie basis, I conclude that 
Life has established that Mediclinic is a dominant firm at each of its hospitals  and a 
monopolist provider of access to and storage facilities at each of its hospitals. It is able 
to exert market power to foreclose rival dialysis service providers from its hospitals. In 
the hospitals referred to in these proceedings, it has done so. It has also been 
established that there has been an anti -competitive effect, at least on a prima facie 
basis and that Life has been completely foreclosed from operating in the specified 
hospitals (Mediclinic Vergelegen, Mediclinic Morningside, Mediclinic Panorama, 
Mediclinic Potchefstroom  and Mediclinic Newcastle ) and that it will ultimately be 
excluded from all Mediclinic’s hospitals, as is its expressed intention. That is because 
the market structure has changed. What was previously essentially an uncontested 
market, has become an incontestable one. 
 
[39] I thus conclude that Life’s complaint is at least plausible. It is not necessary for 
Life to prove at this juncture that its complaint will succeed. It is enough that Life has 
established at least a prima facie case. For present purposes it is not necessary to 
determine which of the provisions of s 8 have been established on a prima facie basis. 
That determination is best left to the Tribunal to consider and determine in due course. 
At the very least  it can be accepted on a prima facie basis that Life has established 
that Mediclinic has engaged in an exclusionary act, other than those described in 
s  8(1)(d) and that the anti -competitive effect of the act outweighs its technological, 
efficiency or other pro-competitive gain as envisaged in s 8(1)(c) or s 8(1)(d)(i). It may 
well be that Life in due course may not be able to establish tying, as required for 
purposes of s 8(1) (d)(iii). That is not fatal to the present relief. The reasoning and 
conclusion of the minority of the Tribunal on this issue cannot be faulted. 
 
[40] However, that is not the end of the enquiry. Both the majority and minority 
members of the Tribunal failed to engage on the remaining factors in s 49C(2)(b). For 
that reason alone , the Trib unal’s decision falls to be set aside.  It is necessary to 
consider the other two factors referred to in s 49C(2). 
 
[41] Turning to the requirement of the need to prevent irreparable or serious ha rm: 
Life’s case is that its competitive position would be irreparably harmed as it would be 
excluded from providing its services at any Mediclin ic hospital until final adjudication 
20 
 
of its complaint, forcing it to re -enter the market as a ne w entrant, requiring the re-
establishment of relationships with referring doctors and new staff. Re-entry would be 
a slow, costly and capital-intensive process and would depend on the availability of 
employees with scarce skills who are in short supply. Life Renal ’s units servicing 
Mediclinic hospitals would cease to operate and the employees of those units would 
leave their employ ; employees who are in short supply and exceptionally valuable. 
Mediclinic did not strenuously dispute this. 
 
[42] The effect of being completely foreclosed from competing for patients in 
Mediclinic’s hospitals from which Life Renal , constitutes a well -grounded 
apprehension of harm, even if there is some doubt as to whether a contravention has 
been established.30 Life’s exclusion would have a n obvious and serious effect on its 
ability to compete, which cannot be repaired by an order in due course simply restoring 
its ability to compete prospectively. That constitutes sufficient harm for the interim relief 
sought by Life.  
 
[43] A further well-grounded apprehension of harm would occur by the channelling 
away of patients who require ongoing outpatient treatment after hospitalisation if the 
crash landers are a significant source of new referrals of new chronic patients.  
Mediclinic acknowledged that providing acute and chronic services in hospital provides 
a good launching pad to expand into the provision of outpatients.  
 
[44] Mediclinic’s argument that the high water mark of Life’s case on harm is that it 
stands to lose revenue is an oversimplification of its case. Its further contention that it 
was incumbent on Life to quantify the revenue at issue , does not pass muster. The 
case is about competitive harm, not merely a loss of revenue.  The facts, considered 
in context, do illustrate irreparable harm to Life’s competitive position.  
 
[45] Turning to the balance of convenience  it requires w eighing the prejudice Life 
would suffer if the interim relief were not granted to Life against the prejudice Mediclinic 
would suffer if interim relief were to be granted . It requires an equitable reckoning as 
 
30Lottoland SA (Pty) Ltd v Google Ireland Ltd and Google SA (Pty) Ltd  (case no IR191Mar23) (12 
November 2024) (Lottoland) para 39. 
21 
 
to who bears the greater burden of error. 31 Prejudice is reckoned by recourse to the 
consequences for the competitive positioning of the parties in the market. As stated in 
Business Connexion: ‘[a] respondent that is required to desist from conduct that gives 
it a legitimate competitive advantage suffers prejudice. An applicant that is required to 
endure an unlawful competitive disadvantage also suffers prejudice’.32 
 
[46] On the facts, Life has  established a favourable balance of convenience . 
Mediclinic did not establish that it would suffer any material harm. On the undisputed 
facts, it would not be precluded from entering and operating concurrently with Life 
Renal in any Mediclinic hospital. The potential harm to patients who require dialysis in 
hospitals must also be taken into consideration. It is irrelevant that private healthcare 
services are involved. Harm to patients is an important consideration because it affects 
patients’ constitutional right of access to healthcare. As confirmed by the Constitutional 
Court, the Constitution imposes a positive duty on a court to promote the spirit, purport 
and objects of the right. 33 That duty is reflected in the Act itself  – maintaining or 
increasing the scope for choice of essential and much needed services.  It is beyond 
dispute that, as found by the minority of the Tribunal: ‘patients that need dialysis are 
severely compromised from a health perspective’ and ‘are a vulnerable group’ . 
Competition between different service providers may well result in an improved quality 
and price of services.  
 
[47] Seen holistically, Life has met the requirements of s 49C(2)(b). This Court must 
exercise its discretion whether to grant an interim order. In considering the various 
factors holistically and taking into account the jurisprudential and transformative 
principles of the Constitution and the Act and the aspiration to create a ‘social justice-
sensitive economy’,34 it would be reasonable and just to exercise such discretion in 
favour of Life. 
 
[48] For these reasons the appeal must be upheld. It would serve no purpose to 
simply substitute the Tribunal’s order with the proposed order, given the passage of 
 
31Business Connexion fn 29 para 158. 
32Business Connexion fn 29 para 22. 
33Mediclinic fn 4 para 72. 
34Mediclinic fn 4 para 2. See also eMedia para 95. 
22 
 
time. It would be fair and reasonable to grant relief with effect from the date of this 
order. Costs follow the result. Given the complexities involved, the employment of two 
counsel was justified.  
 
Order 
[49] In the result, the following order is granted: 
1 The appeal is upheld with costs, including the costs of two counsel; 
2 The decision of the Tribunal dismissing the application is set aside and replaced 
with the following order with effect from date of this order: 
‘1 For a period of six months from the date of this order, or the conclusion of a 
hearing in respect of the prohibited practice s alleged by the applicants in the 
complaint filed with the Competition Commission under case number 
2025FEB0007, whichever is the earlier: 
1.1 The first respondent is directed to reinstate the second applicant’s access 
permissions and on -site storage at Mediclinic Vergelegen, Mediclinic 
Morningside, Mediclinic Panorama, Mediclinic Potchefstroom and Mediclinic 
Newcastle (the hospitals) on the same bases that applied at the time when the 
second applicant operated at the hospitals, and to ensure that the second 
applicant is permitted to administer renal dialysis treatment and/or 
extracorporeal blood-related treatment to patients at the hospitals , where the 
second applicant has been requested to administer such treatment by a 
referring clinician, subject to the second applicant’s substantial adherence to 
the first respondent’s reasonable infection control, security and other protocols;  
1.2 The first respondent is directed to permit the second applicant to continue 
to administer any form of inpatient renal dialysis treatment and/or 
extracorporeal blood-related treatment to patients at all Mediclinic hospitals in 
South Africa at which the second applicant is currently providing services, on 
the same bases as the second applicant currently provides those services, and 
to refrain from in any way preventing or impeding the second applicant from 
doing so, where the second applicant has been req uested to administer such 
treatment by a referring clinician, subject to the second applicant’s continued 
substantial adherence to the first respondent’s reasonable infection control, 
security and other protocols;  
23 
 
1.3 The first respondent is directed to circulate a communication to all clinicians, 
including but not limited to nephrologists, physicians, nurses and renal 
technologists, and to hospital executive and clinical management, at all the 
Mediclinic hospitals at which the second applicant is currently providing 
services, or has been excluded from providing services by the first respondent, 
explaining the nature and meaning of the obligations set out in paragraphs 1.1 
and 1.2 above, and expressly indicating that all clinicians are free to call for the 
services of the second applicant to treat patients at Mediclinic hospitals, and 
that they will not suffer any repercussions as a result of exercising their clinical 
discretion in this regard; and  
1.4 The first respondent is directed to circulate a communication to all 
employees of the second respondent explaining the obligations set out in 
paragraphs 1.1 and 1.2 above, and indicating that the second applicant is 
permitted to treat patients at all the M ediclinic hospitals at which it is currently 
providing services, or has been excluded from providing services by the first 
respondent, and should not be prevented or impeded from carrying out services 
in these hospitals, in any way whatsoever.  
1.5 The costs of the application, including the costs of two counsel, shall be 
paid by the respondents, jointly and severally, the one paying, the other to be 
absolved.’
